title: Change a tire with no breaker bar (cheater pipe)
mechanism_check: Lug nuts are torqued to ~100 ft-lbs; the factory wrench is short, so you need leverage, not strength.
Park on flat solid ground, set the parking brake, and chock a wheel before lifting.
Loosen lugs BEFORE jacking the wheel off the ground.
improvised_tools: A length of pipe slipped over the lug wrench handle as a cheater bar.
Your body weight on the wrench end (bounce gently, never jump).
Penetrating oil on rusted studs, 10 minutes.
steps: Chock wheels, parking brake on, car in park/gear.
Break each lug nut loose a half-turn while the tire is on the ground.
Jack the car at the marked jack point until the tire clears.
Remove lugs, swap the wheel, hand-thread all lugs before lowering.
Lower, then tighten lugs in a star pattern with the cheater pipe — firm, not heroic.
stop_conditions: Car shifting on the jack: stop and re-seat on solid flat ground — never work under a car on a jack alone.
Lug nut rounding or stud spinning: stop before it shears; that's shop equipment territory.

title: Remove a stuck oil filter without a filter wrench
mechanism_check: Spin-on filters thread onto a hollow stud and seal with a rubber gasket; overtightening or heat cycles seize them.
The filter body is thin sheet metal — it crushes before the threads break loose.
improvised_tools: A leather belt or rubber strap looped around the filter as a strap wrench.
A large screwdriver driven straight through the filter body as a turning bar (destroys the filter — only when replacing).
Sandpaper for grip on an oily filter can.
steps: Try the belt strap-wrench first, turning counterclockwise viewed from below.
If it slips, drive a long screwdriver through the filter body near its base and use it as a bar.
Unscrew slowly; have the drain pan positioned — oil will run down your arm.
Before installing the new filter: oil the gasket, thread by hand until the gasket seats, then 3/4 turn more — no wrench.
stop_conditions: Filter base tearing away from the threaded plate: stop — the threaded stub needs professional extraction.
Engine hot: let it cool — oil burns are the main hazard here, not the filter.

title: Pop a hood with a broken release cable
mechanism_check: The hood latch is a spring-loaded claw; the cable pulls the release lever. Broken cable = reach the lever directly.
Have someone press down on the hood while you work — it unloads the latch spring.
improvised_tools: A long flat screwdriver or coat-hanger hook fed through the grille.
A flashlight to see the latch; a second person to press the hood.
steps: Have a helper press down firmly on the hood front edge.
Feed the screwdriver through the grille to the latch mechanism.
Push or pry the release lever sideways (direction varies — feel for the cable's old path).
Lift the hood the moment the latch clicks; prop it securely.
stop_conditions: Latch buried behind a sealed grille with no access: stop — forcing the grille breaks expensive trim.
Hood flies up while driving later: if the latch is damaged, wire it shut and drive straight to repair.

title: Temporary repair of a split radiator hose
mechanism_check: Cooling systems run pressurized (~15 psi) and hot — a split hose sprays scalding coolant.
The repair only needs to hold enough pressure to limp to a shop, not to last.
Never open a hot radiator cap — the system stays pressurized until cool.
improvised_tools: Self-fusing silicone tape or duct tape wrapped tightly over the split, extending well past both ends.
A hose clamp or zip ties over the tape; a rag as a first pressure layer.
Water to top up the system after the repair.
steps: Let the engine cool completely — touch-test the hose before working.
Dry the hose, wrap the split with tape stretched tight, 2 inches past each end.
Clamp or zip-tie over the tape; top up coolant/water.
Drive gently to the nearest repair point with the heater on full (adds cooling) and watch the temp gauge.
stop_conditions: Hose burst wide open or the repair bulges under pressure: stop — it will blow again, get a tow.
Temperature gauge climbing into the red: shut the engine off immediately — a warped head costs more than a tow.

title: Replace a wiper blade with no tools
mechanism_check: Most blades attach with a J-hook, pin, or push-button tab — the arm end tells you which.
The blade is a consumable: the rubber edge, not the frame, does the work.
improvised_tools: Hands only; a rag to protect the windshield when the bare arm is up.
The new blade's packaging usually diagrams the attachment.
steps: Lift the arm and lay a rag on the windshield — a snapped-back bare arm cracks glass.
Find the release tab on the old blade, press it, and slide the blade off the hook.
Slide the new blade on until the tab clicks.
Lower gently and test with washer fluid.
stop_conditions: Arm spring too strong to hold safely: get a second pair of hands — a cracked windshield dwarfs the wiper cost.
Wrong blade length or attachment: don't force it; exchange for the right one.

title: Find a slow tire leak with soapy water
mechanism_check: Slow leaks come from: tread punctures, bead corrosion, valve stems, or cracked valve cores.
Bubbles mark the leak exactly — the soap film makes escaping air visible.
improvised_tools: Dish soap + water in a spray bottle or sponged on.
A valve-core tool or small screwdriver to tighten a loose core; spit on the valve as a quick core test.
steps: Inflate the tire to spec first — leaks show best at pressure.
Spray soapy water over the tread, sidewalls, bead edge, and valve.
Watch for growing bubbles; mark each leak with chalk.
Tighten a bubbling valve core; punctures in the tread get a plug kit or a shop patch.
stop_conditions: Sidewall puncture or bulge: stop — sidewalls can't be patched; the tire is done.
Bead leak from a corroded rim: the wheel needs cleaning/sealing at a shop.

title: Remove a stripped lug nut
mechanism_check: Lug nuts strip from impact guns or wrong-size sockets; the nut is hardened steel on a softer stud.
The wheel must stay on the ground while you break it loose.
improvised_tools: A 12-point socket one size SMALL hammered onto the rounded nut.
Penetrating oil on the stud threads; a cheater pipe for leverage.
A cold chisel to split the nut as a last resort (protect the wheel).
steps: Soak the stud with penetrating oil.
Hammer the undersized 12-point socket firmly onto the nut.
Break it loose with the wheel on the ground, using the cheater pipe.
Replace the damaged nut and inspect the stud threads before reinstalling.
stop_conditions: Stud spinning in the hub: stop — the hub needs professional repair.
Socket splitting or nut cracking unevenly: stop before fragments damage the wheel.

title: Clean and tighten corroded battery terminals
mechanism_check: White/green crust on terminals is corrosion raising resistance — the car cranks slow or clicks.
Always disconnect negative FIRST and reconnect it LAST — this prevents shorting your wrench to ground.
Batteries vent hydrogen: no sparks, no flames near the battery.
improvised_tools: Baking soda + water paste and an old toothbrush or wire brush.
A wrench for the terminal clamps; petroleum jelly to protect after cleaning.
Sandpaper for heavy corrosion on the posts.
steps: Negative cable off first, then positive.
Scrub posts and clamps with baking-soda paste until shiny metal shows.
Rinse with a damp rag (don't flood the battery top), dry fully.
Reconnect positive first, then negative; tighten snug; coat with petroleum jelly.
stop_conditions: Battery case cracked, bulging, or leaking: stop — replace the battery, don't service it.
Terminal post loose in the case: the battery is done; tightening harder breaks the seal.

title: Improve night visibility: restore cloudy headlights
mechanism_check: Cloudy lenses are UV-degraded plastic, not dirt — the haze is in the surface layer.
Restoration is abrasion (remove haze) + polish + UV seal; skipping the seal means re-hazing in months.
improvised_tools: Toothpaste (mild abrasive) or baking-soda paste + a rag for light haze.
Wet sandpaper progression (800-1500-2500) for heavy yellowing; masking tape to protect paint.
A UV sealant or clear-coat wipe as the final step.
steps: Mask the paint around the lens with tape.
Wet-sand through the grits, keeping the surface wet, until the haze is gone.
Polish with toothpaste/paste until clear.
Apply UV sealant and let it cure — this is what makes the fix last.
stop_conditions: Haze inside the lens (condensation): the seal is broken — the housing needs replacing, not polishing.
Lens cracked: polishing a cracked lens is wasted effort; replace it.
